title: The Holy Spirit
hookLine: the Comforter, the one who comes alongside (John 14:26)

cards: You're standing alone in a courtroom, accused, and you don't know the law. You don't know what to say. Your hands are shaking.
Then the door opens, and someone walks in and stands right beside you. They lean over and whisper: I'm here. I'll speak for you.
I'll help you remember what to say. Or think of a hospital bed at night, and someone pulling up a chair. A kid on the first day of school, and an older kid who sits down next to them at lunch.
That movement, someone coming to stand beside you, is inside today's word. It's the name Jesus gives the Holy Spirit on the night before he dies.

teach.b: Paraclete comes from the Greek parakletos. Para, beside, as in parallel. Kletos, called.
One called to stand beside you. In a Greek courtroom, it was the word for a friend or advocate who spoke up for you.
At the Last Supper, in John's Gospel, Jesus tells his frightened friends he's leaving, but they won't be left alone.
"But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you."
He calls the Spirit "another Comforter." Another, because Jesus himself has been one. In First John, Jesus is called our advocate with the Father: the same Greek word.
Translators have wrestled with it for centuries: advocate, helper, counselor, comforter. The King James chose Comforter.
In older English, comfort came from the Latin for with strength. To comfort someone was to strengthen them, not just to soothe them. So the Paraclete isn't only a warm blanket.
It's a friend at your side who makes you strong enough to stand.
Christians say the Holy Spirit is the third person of the Trinity, fully God: the one who hovered over the waters in Genesis, came like a dove at Jesus's baptism and like fire at Pentecost.

teach.h: HE SHALL TEACH YOU ALL THINGS.
teach.b: East and West still differ on exactly how the Spirit proceeds; that's the filioque, from day two hundred eighty-six. But all of them pray the same thing: that the Comforter comes.

how: Christians pray to the Holy Spirit especially at Pentecost, at baptisms and confirmations, and before reading scripture, often with old hymns such as "Come, Holy Ghost, our souls inspire."

o: one called to your side, to help and speak up
an angel sent to carry a message from God
a priest who offers the people's prayers to God

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: a friend or advocate who spoke up for you.
in older English, to comfort meant only to soothe
it came from the Latin for with strength: to make someone strong.
the same Greek word is used of Jesus in First John

games.q: it's the Last Supper. Jesus tells his friends he's leaving. they're frightened. what does he promise?
o: that he'll be back in a week.
another Comforter, who will teach them and help them remember.
that they won't need anyone now.
games.why: he promises the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, who "shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance."

practice: Think of where you feel alone right now, or where you need strength, and don't hurry past it. Then picture someone coming to stand right beside you: not fixing it, just there at your side, making you strong enough to stay.
If you pray, ask the Holy Spirit, the Comforter, to come; if you don't, let that picture keep you company.

wordCard.voice: Paraclete. From the Greek, one called to your side: advocate, helper, comforter. Jesus's name for the Holy Spirit.

orig.note: Greek: one called to your side. An advocate or helper: John's word for the Holy Spirit.

carryVoice: Your line: the comforter comes. Comfort, in the old sense: strength at your side. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you.
